title: Counseling

jokes.text: Jim explains they're late every day because of the daycare across town, then immediately pivots: 'Why didn't I think of this before? Did you know that there is a daycare center opening right here in this building?'
jokes.setup: Jim sympathetically explains the hardship of the daycare being across town causing them to be late every day
jokes.punchline: Jim's 'why didn't I think of this before' reveals he's immediately pivoting to pitch a money-making scheme rather than solving the commute problem — exposing Dwight's landlord opportunism in the same breath
jokes.explanation: Solid setup that recontextualizes the mundane complaint as a business opportunity. The pivot is quick and character-appropriate for Dwight as building owner, but the joke is somewhat telegraphed.

jokes.text: 'Well, I guess it's not an evil idea, it's just a regular idea, but there's no good laugh for a regular idea.'
jokes.setup: Dwight is pitching the daycare center with enthusiasm
jokes.punchline: Dwight meta-commentates that the idea isn't sinister enough to be funny, breaking the fourth wall in a very Dwight-specific way
jokes.explanation: This is a genuinely clever meta joke that could only come from Dwight — he's self-aware enough to know that a normal business idea isn't his brand, and he openly laments it. The joke breaks the fourth wall in a way that feels organic rather than forced. It's funny because Dwight is essentially acknowledging his own villain tendencies while being weirdly self-deprecating. Strong originality and character specificity.

jokes.text: 'You remember my cousin Mose?' — Mose is revealed to be the daycare attendant, standing there with 'Welcome, children.'
jokes.setup: Dwight is giving a tour of his new daycare center, which is meant to seem legitimate
jokes.punchline: Mose — a feral, terrifying man who lives on Schrute Farms — is revealed as the childcare worker, greeting children
jokes.explanation: The horror of Mose being around children is entirely implicit but lands hard for anyone familiar with the character. Strong character integration — this joke only works because the audience knows Mose is essentially a feral human. The 'Welcome, children' delivered earnestly makes it land.

jokes.text: 'Were you painting in the dark?' — Pam's reaction to the daycare's decor, presumably chaotic/crude wall art
jokes.setup: Dwight has decorated the daycare center, presumably with his own aesthetic sensibilities
jokes.punchline: Pam's bewildered question implies the decor looks like it was done blindly — a reaction beat that lets the audience imagine the horror
jokes.explanation: A solid visual-inferential joke. We don't see the art but Pam's line tells us everything we need. Functional but not exceptional.

jokes.text: The 'magical toy box' turns out to contain forks, knives, and a soy sauce packet from the break room
jokes.setup: Dwight grandly introduces the 'magical toy box' as part of the daycare tour
jokes.punchline: Jim identifies them as utensils from the office break room; Dwight reframes them as 'Mister Fork, Lieutenant Knife, and Miss Fork'
jokes.explanation: The naming of the utensils — 'Mister Fork, Lieutenant Knife, and Miss Fork' — is a delightful Dwight-ism. The military rank for the knife but not the forks is a perfect absurdist detail. It builds on Jim's deadpan calling-out, and the escalation to the soy sauce packet adds another layer.

jokes.text: 'And a soy sauce packet.' / 'That shouldn't have been in there. I'm embarrassed.'
jokes.setup: Dwight has just defended the fork and knife as legitimate children's toys with imaginative names
jokes.punchline: Jim finds a soy sauce packet, which Dwight cannot defend — and his genuine embarrassment about specifically the soy sauce (not the knives) is the joke
jokes.explanation: This is a beautifully structured beat. Dwight has an elaborate defense for the knives and forks, but the soy sauce packet breaks him. His genuine embarrassment about the packet — not the dangerous cutlery — is perfectly inverted logic. The economy is excellent: Jim's flat delivery and Dwight's short mortified response do maximum work in minimum words.

jokes.text: Dwight describes the daycare as having a 'feeding trough' and a 'play bucket,' and says the door 'locks from the outside — escape is impossible'
jokes.setup: Dwight is listing the daycare's amenities in the manner of a legitimate facility
jokes.punchline: 'The door locks from the outside. Escape is impossible.' — delivered as a selling point
jokes.explanation: Deeply Dwight. The accumulation of 'feeding trough' and 'play bucket' builds perfectly to 'escape is impossible,' which Dwight says with total sincerity as though it's a safety feature parents want. The character integration here is near-perfect — only Dwight would think this is reassuring. Highly quotable.

jokes.text: Jim says 'Prove it' when Dwight claims the door locks, leading Dwight into the room; Jim and Pam then lock him in
jokes.setup: Dwight brags that the door locks from the outside and escape is impossible
jokes.punchline: Jim tricks Dwight into demonstrating by going inside, then locks him in; Dwight's protests from inside confirm the lock works
jokes.explanation: Classic Jim-and-Pam prank teamwork, well-executed. Dwight's own boast becomes the weapon used against him. Good structural payoff, though the prank type is familiar territory for the show.

jokes.text: 'No one. The door locks from the outside. Escape is impossible.' — Dwight on child supervision
jokes.setup: Pam asks who will be watching the children
jokes.punchline: Dwight's answer treats childcare as a containment problem, not a safety/nurturing one — the door locks from the outside and escape is impossible
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best jokes. The deadpan delivery of 'Escape is impossible' as a selling point for a daycare is perfectly dark and character-specific. Only Dwight frames child supervision as a prison logistics problem. Economy is exceptional — three sentences, maximum horror. Highly quotable.

jokes.text: Michael's counseling session opens with him yelling 'This is the worst! You are the worst. I hate looking at your face. I wanna smash it!'
jokes.setup: Michael has been assigned mandatory counseling with Toby, whom he despises
jokes.punchline: Michael's opening statement to his therapist is a full-throated emotional attack on the therapist's face
jokes.explanation: Michael's hatred of Toby is a running gag, and this is a solid expression of it. The context of a therapy session makes the hostility funnier. Character-specific and energetic, though not surprising given established dynamics.

jokes.text: Toby's talking head: 'I actually have a degree in social work. I mean, I know a lot of people would just ask a few standard questions and tick off a few boxes, but I've got a chance to do some good here.'
jokes.setup: Toby talks to the camera about the opportunity he has with Michael's counseling
jokes.punchline: The audience knows Michael will never meaningfully engage, making Toby's genuine optimism tragically ironic and funny
jokes.explanation: Classic Toby — earnest and doomed. The joke is entirely in dramatic irony; we know exactly how wrong he is. Functional but not exceptional.

jokes.text: Michael: 'I know what you wanna ask me. Did your mom ever see you naked?' / 'So you can molest me?'
jokes.setup: Toby tries to begin the counseling session professionally
jokes.punchline: Michael projects outrageous paranoia onto Toby, first assuming sexual questions, then accusing him of planning molestation when Toby suggests privacy
jokes.explanation: Michael's paranoia about therapy is well-characterized, and the escalation from 'naked' to molestation accusations is rapid and character-appropriate. Slightly cheap but executed with energy.

jokes.text: Michael insists on leaving the blinds open 'so everybody can see what a big failure you are' — referring to Toby, not himself
jokes.setup: Michael refuses to close the blinds for privacy during his mandatory counseling
jokes.punchline: He frames keeping the blinds open as exposing Toby's failure, completely inverting who is being counseled
jokes.explanation: Michael's total lack of self-awareness is perfectly captured here. He genuinely believes Toby is the one being exposed as a failure. The inversion is clean and character-specific.

jokes.text: 'Boycott the Steamtown Mall! Everyone, you heard me. Cancel all your business with the Steamtown Mall!'
jokes.setup: Dwight storms into the office clearly upset
jokes.punchline: His response to being humiliated at a store is to declare a full boycott of an entire mall, with no context given
jokes.explanation: Dwight's disproportionate response is classic. The fact that he withholds all context while demanding solidarity is very in-character. Good energy, predictable Dwight escalation.

jokes.text: Jim: 'The mall itself, or the stores in the mall?' / Dwight: 'All of it! The mall, the stores, the kiosks.'
jokes.setup: Dwight has declared a boycott of the Steamtown Mall
jokes.punchline: Jim's pedantic clarifying question and Dwight's furious comprehensive answer treat a petty personal grievance as geopolitical strategy
jokes.explanation: Jim's deadpan precision and Dwight's indignant comprehensiveness play perfectly off each other. The escalation to 'the kiosks' is a nice specific detail that elevates the joke.

jokes.text: 'America's one big mall.'
jokes.setup: Dwight has declared a sweeping boycott of all malls
jokes.punchline: Kevin's flat, philosophical non-sequitur cuts through the hysteria with accidental profundity
jokes.explanation: Five words, maximum impact. Kevin's throwaway observation accidentally makes a sharp point while completely deflating Dwight's drama. The economy is nearly perfect — any more words would ruin it. This is the kind of Kevin moment that rewards his character being in the scene.

jokes.text: Toby describes his peaceful place as 'the walk from the yogurt shop to my car, after I drop my daughter off on Sunday afternoons'
jokes.setup: Toby is using a therapy technique, asking Michael to imagine a peaceful place, and shares his own example
jokes.punchline: Toby's 'peaceful place' is the walk after dropping off his daughter during divorced-dad weekend — a deeply melancholy image of a man at peace only when briefly alone
jokes.explanation: This is one of the best Toby jokes in the episode. It's funny and sad simultaneously — his happiest moment is the brief solitude after fulfilling his parental obligation. Perfectly character-integrated. The specificity of the yogurt shop elevates it beyond a generic 'sad Toby' joke.

jokes.text: Jim's talking head: 'I'm glad Michael's getting help. He has a lot of issues, and he's stupid.'
jokes.setup: Jim speaks diplomatically to the camera about Michael's mandatory counseling
jokes.punchline: After a measured, empathetic opener, Jim bluntly adds '...and he's stupid' as a coda
jokes.explanation: The structure is simple but effective: measured diplomatic framing punctured by pure bluntness. The pause before 'and he's stupid' is where the laugh lives. Classic Jim confessional economy.

jokes.text: Pam's cold call: 'Look, I'm not gonna tell you that we have lower prices. Is price something that is important to you?' [pause] 'Okay, well, let me know if anything changes.'
jokes.setup: Pam is struggling as a salesperson making cold calls
jokes.punchline: Her pitch is so bad she essentially argues against her own product, then gives up when the customer isn't interested, signing off politely on a failed call
jokes.explanation: The anti-pitch is beautifully awkward. 'I'm not going to tell you we have lower prices' followed immediately by asking if price matters is perfect cringe logic. 'Let me know if anything changes' is a delightful defeated sign-off. Strong character work — Pam is too honest and too nice to sell.

jokes.text: Pam asks Jim: 'Tell me everything's gonna be okay.' / 'Tell me I'm good at sales.' Jim unconvincingly complies both times.
jokes.setup: Pam is clearly failing at sales and needs reassurance
jokes.punchline: Jim's hollow, halting 'You're good... you're good at sales' reveals he cannot honestly endorse her abilities, even for her sake
jokes.explanation: Sweet and funny. Jim's hesitation says everything. The double 'you're good' with the pause in the middle is a well-performed beat. Relies on performance more than writing.

jokes.text: Pam's talking head: 'The unfair thing about working in sales is that your salary is almost all commission. So if you suck at sales, you make almost no money. I guess that's fair.'
jokes.setup: Pam complains about commission-based salary being unfair to bad salespeople
jokes.punchline: She immediately talks herself out of her complaint mid-sentence, arriving at 'I guess that's fair' with complete sincerity
jokes.explanation: One of the best jokes in the episode. The structure is airtight: complaint, logic, self-defeat, acceptance. 'I guess that's fair' is earned because we've watched her reason through her own grievance and arrive at her opponent's conclusion. It's deeply Pam — self-aware, slightly defeated, quietly funny. Maximum economy. Highly quotable.

jokes.text: Dwight confirms he called Jim's clients at the mall and used 'the f-word' on their behalf, as if it were an act of loyalty
jokes.setup: Jim confronts Dwight about canceling his business with mall clients
jokes.punchline: Dwight confirms it matter-of-factly, framing sabotage as solidarity, and announces he'll do the same to all Jim's clients
jokes.explanation: Dwight's oblivious aggression is well-deployed. The specificity of 'the f-word' as a euphemism Dwight used professionally is a nice touch. Character-consistent escalation.

jokes.text: Dwight: 'That mall is corrupt. Okay, they're appearancist!'
jokes.setup: Dwight is defending his boycott of the mall
jokes.punchline: Dwight coins the word 'appearancist' — a portmanteau of appearance and racist — as a legitimate grievance category
jokes.explanation: Dwight coining new vocabulary is one of his best recurring bits. 'Appearancist' is a genuinely funny neologism that captures his way of seeing the world — always formalizing grievances into systems. Quotable and character-specific.

jokes.text: Dwight's backstory: He took Mose to the mall 'to get his blood pressure at the Rite Aid' and saw something in a fancy store window
jokes.setup: Dwight explains why he was at the mall to begin with
jokes.punchline: The inciting errand — taking his feral cousin to get a blood pressure reading at a pharmacy — is treated as completely normal
jokes.explanation: The detail of taking Mose to get his blood pressure checked is quietly absurd and perfectly in-world. It's a throwaway line that rewards attention.

jokes.text: Dwight: 'I guess I'm not the kind of guy that's good enough for precious heirlooms.'
jokes.setup: Dwight describes being ignored and photographed by store staff when he pressed the buzzer to enter a luxury store
jokes.punchline: He describes whatever he wanted to buy as 'precious heirlooms' — the grandiosity of the description vs. the reality (later revealed to be a pewter wizard) is the joke
jokes.explanation: The word 'heirlooms' does a lot of work setting up the later reveal of the pewter wizard. On rewatch it's even funnier knowing what he's talking about. Solid misdirection planted early.

jokes.text: Kelly: 'We should start our own mall.' / Andy: 'Yeah!' / Jim: 'Wait, wait, wait. Actually, that's a really good idea, Kelly.' / Kelly: 'What did I say? I talk a lot, so I've learned to just tune myself out.'
jokes.setup: The group is brainstorming alternatives to Dwight's boycott
jokes.punchline: Kelly's offhand suggestion is praised, but she literally doesn't remember what she said because she tunes herself out
jokes.explanation: 'I talk a lot, so I've learned to just tune myself out' is a brilliant Kelly line — it perfectly captures her self-awareness about her own verbal output while being completely absurd. It's highly quotable and could only come from Kelly. One of the episode's best character comedy moments.

jokes.text: Dwight: 'No, you and I... and I.' — correcting Jim when Jim volunteers himself to accompany Dwight to the store
jokes.setup: Jim offers to go with Dwight to confront the store; Dwight initially resists including Jim
jokes.punchline: Dwight's grammatical self-correction — 'No, you and I... and I' — is a nonsensical reassertion of his primacy that makes no grammatical sense
jokes.explanation: Short and sharp. Dwight's instinct to correct and assert dominance even when it results in grammatical nonsense is perfect character comedy. The joke is in the broken logic delivered with total confidence.

jokes.text: Gabe's talking head: 'Did you assume that I would automatically side with the rich, snobby shop owner? How about now?' — implying he looks like or is one
jokes.setup: Gabe addresses the camera as if responding to an assumption about him
jokes.punchline: The 'how about now' — presumably accompanied by a gesture or expression — suggests he's revealing something about himself that confirms the assumption
jokes.explanation: Mildly funny Gabe self-deprecation, but the joke is incomplete without the visual. Hard to fully evaluate from transcript alone. Functional.

jokes.text: Michael cuts Toby off mid-sentence: 'One hour. We've done one hour. Let's just speed this up. Okay, keep it moving. I wanna do all six hours today.'
jokes.setup: Toby is beginning a gentle therapeutic question
jokes.punchline: Michael treats the mandatory counseling like a prison sentence to be served as quickly as possible, demanding they rush through five remaining hours
jokes.explanation: Michael's strategy of trying to serve his therapy sentence like jail time is wonderfully absurd and character-perfect. 'Keep it moving' applied to emotional processing is funny.

jokes.text: Michael: 'Be careful what you wish for, Toby.' — said as an ominous threat before beginning to talk
jokes.setup: Toby has finally gotten Michael to agree to talk during the session
jokes.punchline: Michael issues a dramatic villain-style warning about his own upcoming talking, as if sharing his feelings is a weapon
jokes.explanation: Michael treating emotional openness as a threat to Toby is a great inversion. The ominous framing of 'Be careful what you wish for' before launching into presumably bizarre stories is perfectly Michael.

jokes.text: Michael tries to describe the plot of Pretty Woman but doesn't know the title — 'Apparently there's a famous Hollywood movie from the 1980s... beautiful girl.' Everyone has to correct him: 'Pretty Woman.'
jokes.setup: Michael is advising Dwight to do the Pretty Woman revenge move on the shop
jokes.punchline: Michael — who presumably watches a lot of TV and movies — cannot name or accurately describe one of the most famous romantic comedies of all time
jokes.explanation: Michael's inability to name or summarize a famous movie is a reliable character bit. 'Beautiful girl' is a funny wrong answer. The group corrections add to it.

jokes.text: Michael describes Pretty Woman's plot: 'The sex worker is denied service... that can't be right.' / Andy and Jim insist on hearing his version anyway.
jokes.setup: Michael is haltingly describing the plot of Pretty Woman
jokes.punchline: Michael himself is confused by the premise of a movie he apparently has seen, and Andy/Jim deliberately withhold the correction to hear his version
jokes.explanation: The meta-joke of the group wanting to hear Michael's confused version is a nice touch. Andy and Jim's complicity in withholding the correction is good ensemble comedy.

jokes.text: Andy dramatically delivers the 'Big mistake. Huge.' line, cutting off Michael mid-telling
jokes.setup: Michael is recounting the Pretty Woman scene where Julia Roberts tells off the shopgirls
jokes.punchline: Andy can't contain himself and delivers the iconic line himself, stealing Michael's moment
jokes.explanation: Andy's inability to let Michael finish the story, and his proprietary excitement over the punchline, is good character work. The audience's familiarity with the movie line adds to it.

jokes.text: Pam's talking head: 'I.' — a single word, claiming the title of office administrator to a vendor who asked who was in charge
jokes.setup: A vendor asks if someone in the office is the administrator; there's a beat before Pam answers
jokes.punchline: 'I.' — delivered as a single, definitive, slightly over-confident syllable from someone who may not actually have that job
jokes.explanation: One word. Maximum information. The single 'I.' delivered as a confessional talking head is one of the episode's most economical and funniest beats. It captures Pam's growing ambition, her slight scheming, and her self-satisfaction all at once. The pause before it and the grammar — 'I.' not 'Me' — adds a regal quality. Perfect economy score.

jokes.text: Pam stands up and loudly declares: 'I'm the office administrator!'
jokes.setup: Following her quiet 'I.' to the camera, Pam now asserts her claimed title to whoever is listening
jokes.punchline: The escalation from the single whispered 'I.' to the full declarative announcement is a perfect comic escalation of Pam's con

jokes.text: Pam's talking head: 'There are a few ways to get promoted. One is to wait for an opening and apply for it. That's the main way. But this could work.'
jokes.setup: Pam has just claimed to be the office administrator to a vendor
jokes.punchline: Her confessional acknowledges the legitimate path to promotion exists, then endorses her scam alternative with a shrug
jokes.explanation: Beautifully structured. 'That's the main way. But this could work.' is a great button. The casual moral shrug from Pam — typically the show's conscience — is funny because it's slightly out of character. The economy is strong and it lands as a satisfying confessional.

jokes.text: Michael Freudian slips: 'When I was sitting at the table, eating my penis... I mean peas.'
jokes.setup: Michael has agreed to open up to Toby and begins a personal anecdote
jokes.punchline: He Freudian-slips 'penis' before correcting to 'peas'
jokes.explanation: A fairly cheap joke. Freudian slips in TV comedies are a well-worn device, and this one doesn't do much with the setup beyond the shock value. It doesn't reveal anything new about Michael. The 'I mean peas' correction is the most by-the-numbers version of this joke possible. Below average for this show.

jokes.text: Michael claims he was 'probed by an alien life force — an A.L.F. Alf. You know, I might have actually been probed by Alf. You might think he's a puppet, you never see the lower half, but there's a lower half.'
jokes.setup: Michael is ostensibly opening up about his issues to Toby during counseling
jokes.punchline: He goes from alien abduction to specifically Alf the TV puppet, then defends the physical plausibility of Alf having a lower body
jokes.explanation: This is a wonderfully escalating absurdist bit. The pivot from 'alien life force' to the specific 1980s puppet ALF is unexpected, and the meta-analysis of ALF's unseen lower half ('there's a lower half') is the kind of deranged logical extension that makes Michael uniquely funny. The deadpan insistence on ALF's physicality is inspired. This could only be Michael.

jokes.text: Dwight's makeover presentation: 'Before me stands your coworker, Dwight Kurt Schrute. Dwight, show them all sides, turn around.'
jokes.setup: Jim presents Dwight in his makeover outfit to the office
jokes.punchline: Jim speaks about Dwight in the third person while Dwight is standing right there, treating him like a product being unveiled
jokes.explanation: Fun staging, with Jim's infomercial energy contrasting with Dwight's compliance. The third-person presentation is a reliable comedy device used well here.

jokes.text: Kevin/Oscar: 'Your shirt and tie are disgusto-barfo.' — evaluating Dwight's current outfit
jokes.setup: The office is assessing Dwight's current look before the makeover
jokes.punchline: 'Disgusto-barfo' as a compound adjective-descriptor is a Kevin-specific linguistic invention
jokes.explanation: 'Disgusto-barfo' is a great Kevin coinage — childish, emphatic, and completely sincere. Short and effective.

jokes.text: The advice 'not so monochromatic, not so matching' — less matching = more rich — confuses Dwight: 'Wait, less matching to appear more rich?'
jokes.setup: Oscar is giving Dwight fashion advice
jokes.punchline: Dwight's genuine confusion at the counterintuitive logic of fashion — that rich people deliberately mismatch — is funny because it IS actually counterintuitive
jokes.explanation: A nice observational joke about fashion logic wrapped in a Dwight moment. His genuine puzzlement is funny because he's right — it IS weird.

jokes.text: Dwight's glasses are removed; multiple people say they liked them / thought they were cute; Dwight says 'I can't see.'
jokes.setup: The makeover team removes Dwight's glasses as part of the transformation
jokes.punchline: While others aestheticize his glasses, Dwight's only concern is functional: 'I can't see'
jokes.explanation: Dwight's pure practicality cutting through everyone's aesthetic opinions is a solid beat. 'I can't see' is the perfect Dwight response. Not especially original but well-executed.

jokes.text: Dwight: 'Wait, I see you every day. Can I say, "good month?"' — in response to being told to greet people with 'good morning, good afternoon'
jokes.setup: Andy is coaching Dwight to say 'good morning, good afternoon' to people
jokes.punchline: Dwight suggests 'good month' as an alternative for people he sees every day, implying he finds daily greetings redundant
jokes.explanation: 'Good month' is an excellent Dwight line. His logic is internally consistent — if you see someone daily, granular time-of-day greetings are redundant, so why not aggregate? It's a genuinely funny linguistic/social proposal delivered with total earnestness. Highly quotable, great character integration. One of the episode's best lines.

jokes.text: Dwight's acceptance drill: 'Please. / Thank you. / Copy. Thank you. / Please. / I think he's got it.'
jokes.setup: Andy is drilling Dwight on saying please and thank you
jokes.punchline: Dwight responds to 'please' and 'thank you' as if they're radio call codes ('copy'), revealing he's treating social niceties as military protocol
jokes.explanation: 'Copy' as a response to 'please and thank you go a long way' is perfectly Dwight — he acknowledges the information received as tactical data. The escalating thank-you/please exchange ending in 'I think he's got it' is a good comedic button.

jokes.text: Dwight: 'And I was raised by wolves. I was 25 years old before I saw my first human being. Wait, is it a full moon tonight?'
jokes.setup: Dwight is practicing social niceties in the coaching session
jokes.punchline: Out of nowhere, Dwight offers a false backstory about being raised by wolves, then checks if tonight is a full moon — treating lycanthropy as a possible concern
jokes.explanation: The wolf backstory is clearly one of Michael's fake therapy stories being tried out or a Dwight non-sequitur. Either way, the full moon check is a nice extension. Absurdist and in-character.

jokes.text: Michael: 'Yes, yes, they are all fake stories. What sort of twisted mind would come up with weird stories like that? Three hours, we're halfway done.' / Toby: 'How?'
jokes.setup: Toby calls Michael out on his fake therapy stories
jokes.punchline: Michael admits they're all fake, pivots immediately to celebrating his time progress, and Toby's incredulous 'How?' suggests the math doesn't work
jokes.explanation: Toby's 'How?' is the perfect punctuation. Michael's cheerful pivot from admission of lying to time-keeping is great character comedy. The exchange is economical and lands well.

jokes.text: Toby surrenders: 'You know what, Michael? You're right. You win. This is pointless.' Then reveals he has 'fun stuff in case my daughter ever comes over' — a box of children's games in his office
jokes.setup: Michael has worn Toby down completely during the counseling session
jokes.punchline: Toby's sad capitulation is punctuated by the revelation that he keeps children's games in his office for his daughter's visits — which apparently never happen or are so rare he keeps them at work
jokes.explanation: The detail of the children's games in case his daughter 'ever comes over' is heartbreaking and funny simultaneously — a perfect Toby moment. The implication that daughter visits are rare enough that he keeps games at the office is devastating characterization delivered as a casual aside. High character integration.

jokes.text: Dwight's disposable camera talking head: 'Disposable cameras are fun, although it does seem wasteful and you don't ever get to see your pictures. If it's an important event you want to remember, I recommend using a real camera. But I don't care if I forget today.'
jokes.setup: Dwight is about to go on his Pretty Woman revenge mission
jokes.punchline: His review of disposable cameras is weirdly thorough and ends with 'But I don't care if I forget today' — dismissing what should be a triumphant moment
jokes.explanation: Dwight's random product review is a funny non-sequitur, and 'I don't care if I forget today' is a darkly funny button that deflates the revenge mission's importance. Solid but not exceptional.

jokes.text: Michael's story about the baseball game: he felt bad for the pitcher being taken out because 'he wasn't going to be able to play with his friends anymore.' Jeff said the manager was 'making a really good move' — Michael absorbed the abandonment lesson.
jokes.setup: Toby and Michael are unexpectedly connecting over a childhood game; Michael shares a memory of a baseball game with his stepfather Jeff
jokes.punchline: Michael's childlike misinterpretation of a pitching change as a player being separated from his friends reveals deep childhood feelings of abandonment, played as both funny and sad
jokes.explanation: This is one of the episode's best moments — Michael's childlike baseball misunderstanding functions simultaneously as comedy and as surprisingly touching character depth. It reveals that Michael projected his own fears of abandonment onto a pitcher, and that Jeff's approval of 'the manager's move' was Michael desperately seeking validation. The writing earns this by making us laugh and feel something. High character integration — this is entirely Michael.

jokes.text: Toby realizes the counseling is genuinely working: 'It's working. I'm doing it.' — followed by an immediate interruption
jokes.setup: Michael has been opening up about his childhood and Jeff
jokes.punchline: Toby's private celebration of his therapeutic breakthrough is immediately undercut — the audience knows it's about to be destroyed
jokes.explanation: Good dramatic irony beat. Toby's brief triumph is perfectly timed against what we know is coming. The 'Ahem' interruption (probably Jim signaling Dwight) is a nice physical punctuation.

jokes.text: Michael: 'It's very important for you to be liked, isn't it?' / Michael: 'Well, let's not get too... this isn't a counseling session.' / Toby sighs.
jokes.setup: Toby has made a genuine therapeutic breakthrough observation about Michael needing to be liked
jokes.punchline: Michael immediately shuts it down by reminding Toby 'this isn't a counseling session' — in the middle of his mandatory counseling session
jokes.explanation: Brilliant structure. Toby has just identified Michael's core wound — his need to be liked — and Michael's self-protective reflex is to deny that this IS a counseling session while sitting in mandatory counseling. The dramatic irony is perfect: the very act of shutting it down proves the point. Toby's realization ('you son of a gun...') is the cherry on top. Highly quotable line and a standout moment.

jokes.text: Toby: 'Dogs don't do that.' Michael: 'Right? Why would a dog do that?'
jokes.setup: Michael has explained that his dog ran away to find a better kid
jokes.punchline: Toby and Michael briefly bond over agreeing dogs don't do this — Toby as therapist gently correcting, Michael as patient relieved to be told this
jokes.explanation: Nice tag to the dog story. The therapeutic exchange working briefly, with both men momentarily on the same team against the logic of a dog choosing to leave, is gently funny.

jokes.text: Toby's realization: 'You son of a gun.' / then 'You son of a bitch.' — escalating as he realizes what Michael just revealed
jokes.setup: Toby realizes Michael just unwittingly confirmed his deepest need while denying they're in a counseling session
jokes.punchline: Toby escalates from 'you son of a gun' to 'you son of a bitch' — with genuine emotion — as the breakthrough sinks in

jokes.text: Michael turns on Toby viciously: 'You couldn't help your marriage... Nobody needs your help. Nobody wants it. You can't help anybody. I don't need your help. Am I gonna make you cry?'
jokes.setup: Toby's therapeutic breakthrough has frightened Michael, who now lashes out
jokes.punchline: Michael weaponizes Toby's divorce and professional inadequacy to shut down the vulnerable moment, ending with 'Am I gonna make you cry?' — said with both cruelty and almost childish pride
jokes.explanation: The self-protection is very Michael — when he gets close to real vulnerability, he destroys the moment by becoming horrible. 'Am I gonna make you cry?' captures his childish cruelty. Uncomfortable and character-revealing.

jokes.text: Michael: 'Okay, filled out... Good. Thank you, doctor, take two of these and call me in the morning.' — dismissing Toby after the forms are signed
jokes.setup: Toby gives up and asks Michael to fill out the forms himself
jokes.punchline: Michael appropriates the doctor's dismissal line and applies it to Toby — reversing the therapeutic relationship
jokes.explanation: A reasonably fun inversion. Michael calling Toby 'doctor' and using the clinical dismissal is appropriately absurd. Functional but not exceptional.

jokes.text: Pam's talking head about collecting signatures: 'There are a lot of one-person departments here, so there's a lot of department heads. But I'm off to a good start. Oh man, if I can pull this off, it will be the scam of all scams. And yet, very helpful to everyone.'
jokes.setup: Pam is trying to get retroactive paperwork signed for her fabricated office administrator position
jokes.punchline: 'The scam of all scams. And yet, very helpful to everyone.' — Pam frames her fraud as community service
jokes.explanation: 'The scam of all scams. And yet, very helpful to everyone.' is a great button. Pam's self-justifying fraud framed as altruism is funny and reveals her character evolution in this season. The 'and yet' is doing tremendous work.

jokes.text: Corporate has sent Gabe to double-check Michael's evaluation — Toby marked 'severe' in ALL categories, including 'at risk for homicidal behavior'
jokes.setup: Corporate is reviewing Toby's evaluation of Michael's counseling
jokes.punchline: Toby marked 'severe' across all categories including homicidal behavior — the ultimate passive-aggressive revenge after the session
jokes.explanation: Toby's revenge via paperwork is perfectly in-character — the most aggressive he can ever be is administrative. The inclusion of 'at risk for homicidal behavior' as a checked box is the escalating dark comedy beat that makes it land. Great callback to Michael's cruelty.

jokes.text: Gabe confronts Pam about being office administrator: 'I have gone through everything from the past three years. There is nothing that says that you're office administrator.' / Pam: 'So weird that there's no paperwork.'
jokes.setup: Gabe has investigated Pam's claimed title and found no documentation
jokes.punchline: Pam responds to the evidence of her fraud with 'So weird that there's no paperwork' — feigning innocent bewilderment
jokes.explanation: 'So weird that there's no paperwork' is a perfect line. The tone of genuine bewilderment from someone who clearly knows exactly why there's no paperwork is Pam at her best. The audience is totally on her side.

jokes.text: Pam deflects with a story about her Australian friend meeting someone from two streets away: 'Canberra, I think, and she met this guy who lived only two streets away from her in America.'
jokes.setup: Gabe points out there's absolutely no paperwork supporting Pam's claimed role
jokes.punchline: Pam offers an anecdote about a coincidence in Australia as evidence that 'unlikely things happen all the time,' using it to normalize her fraudulent position
jokes.explanation: The Australian coincidence story as a deflection is wonderfully absurd. Pam is using a vaguely related anecdote to argue that improbable things happen, therefore her undocumented promotion might be real. The logical leap is funny and character-specific.

jokes.text: Gabe: 'Statements of such a nature, while they have their place, are overused in a competitive business environment.' — responding to Pam's demand that he make a definitive statement
jokes.setup: Pam demands Gabe either call her a liar or confirm she has the job
jokes.punchline: Gabe responds with corporate non-speak so impenetrable it says nothing, and Pam uses his non-answer to keep her position
jokes.explanation: Gabe's corporate word-salad non-answer is a great character moment and a sharp piece of writing about how corporate cowardice enables bad behavior. Pam wins by default, which is funnier than if she'd argued him down.

jokes.text: Gabe: 'Could I get one of those nameplates that says "Gabe Lewis"?' / Pam: 'For sure. Anything else? I'll get it right away.'
jokes.setup: Gabe just tried and failed to expose Pam's fraudulent title
jokes.punchline: He immediately turns around and uses her as his office administrator to order his nameplate — validating the very position he was trying to dismantle

jokes.text: Pam immediately gets Gabe a nameplate as her first act as office administrator, after winning their confrontation
jokes.setup: Pam has just defeated Gabe's challenge to her authority
jokes.punchline: Pam immediately offers Gabe a nameplate — performing the administrator role she just fought for — and Gabe meekly accepts
jokes.explanation: Nice button on the Pam/Gabe scene. Pam's instant pivot to administrator duties after winning is both triumphant and funny — and Gabe's 'could I get one of those nameplates that says Gabe Lewis?' is the perfect deflated acceptance of defeat.

jokes.text: Pam's talking head: 'The first lesson of watching World Poker Tour at 2:00 A.M.: you play the opponent, not the cards.'
jokes.setup: Pam has just won her standoff with Gabe
jokes.punchline: She cites 2 AM poker television as her strategic inspiration for workplace fraud
jokes.explanation: Excellent Pam confessional. The specificity of 'World Poker Tour at 2:00 A.M.' as her source of business strategy is perfectly absurd and specific. The wisdom itself ('you play the opponent, not the cards') is actually correct, which makes it funnier — she did actually apply it. Strong economy and quotability.

jokes.text: The reveal: the 'precious heirloom' Dwight wanted to buy is a pewter wizard holding a crystal
jokes.setup: For the entire episode, Dwight has been describing the item that caused his humiliation as something important and valuable ('precious heirlooms')
jokes.punchline: The item is revealed to be a pewter wizard holding a crystal — an aggressively tacky fantasy figurine
jokes.explanation: The payoff of the long-running mystery item is excellent. 'A pewter wizard, holding a crystal' is the perfect anti-climactic reveal — both entirely Dwight and completely absurd as a reason to organize a mall boycott. The episode earns this payoff through withholding the information. The character integration is near-perfect: of course this is what Dwight covets.

jokes.text: Jim warns Dwight: 'You know you can't buy that now, right? I can come back and get it for you later, but I'm saying right now, we can't do that.' / Dwight: 'Right. 'Cause I'm here for Revenge.'
jokes.setup: Dwight sees the wizard and is immediately tempted to buy it, forgetting they're supposed to be doing a Pretty Woman revenge move first
jokes.punchline: Dwight's 'I'm here for Revenge' — said like a solemn oath while staring at a fantasy figurine — is funnier for its gravity

jokes.text: The store clerk says: 'Of course I remember him — he looks much less threatening now.' / 'We had a safety concern. We very politely indicated that he'd be welcomed back if he were in accordance with our dress policy.' / 'The bloodstained hands.'
jokes.setup: Dwight launches into his Pretty Woman speech about being denied service
jokes.punchline: The clerk reveals Dwight wasn't refused for being poor — he was refused because his hands were covered in what Dwight explains was beet juice. The entire premise of the boycott was a misunderstanding.
jokes.explanation: This is the episode's best structured payoff. The entire Dwight storyline recontextualizes in one line: he wasn't discriminated against for being poor or looking rough — he had BLOODSTAINED HANDS (beet juice). The store was being reasonable. The episode-long boycott, the moral outrage, the makeover, all of it was based on a misunderstanding. Excellent misdirection planted carefully. 'I'm a beet farmer' is a perfect Dwight explanation.

jokes.text: The store clerk says he remembers Dwight from yesterday and explains they had 'a safety concern' because of 'the bloodstained hands'
jokes.setup: Dwight confronts the clerk who denied him service, expecting snobbery to be the reason
jokes.punchline: It wasn't snobbery — they thought Dwight's beet-stained hands were blood and considered him a safety threat
jokes.explanation: Masterful subversion. The entire episode's A-plot assumes Dwight was treated as a class non-person. The reveal that it was actually Dwight's beet-farming appearance that looked like a crime scene is both a great twist and perfectly in character. 'The bloodstained hands' is a great line. This recontextualizes the whole Pretty Woman scheme as a misunderstanding, which is exactly the kind of ironic structure The Office excels at.

jokes.text: Dwight loses his aristocratic composure and starts yelling at the clerk mid-'big mistake huge' moment; Jim holds him back
jokes.setup: Dwight is executing the Pretty Woman revenge; the store has apologized
jokes.punchline: Dwight can't maintain the composed wealthy-customer persona and collapses into his natural aggressive register, undermining the entire scheme
jokes.explanation: Physical comedy beat that works because of character — Dwight's inability to remain in any persona is consistent. The chaos of the revenge imploding is funny but relies on performance more than writing.

jokes.text: Dwight delivers his version of the 'Big mistake. Huge.' line anyway: 'You made a big mistake! Huge!'
jokes.setup: The Pretty Woman plan has completely fallen apart; there's no legitimate grievance to avenge
jokes.punchline: Dwight delivers the iconic line anyway — desperately, almost pleadingly — as the moral authority of his position has completely collapsed

jokes.text: Jim: 'That was pretty good.' / Dwight: 'Thank you. Please.'
jokes.setup: Jim compliments Dwight's delivery of the line
jokes.punchline: Dwight responds with 'Thank you. Please.' — robotically deploying his etiquette training in sequence

jokes.text: Michael forged and faxed his own counseling evaluation forms, then blames Toby for 'getting him so worked up'
jokes.setup: Toby realizes Michael filled out and faxed his own evaluation forms
jokes.punchline: Michael admits it but claims Toby provoked him into the mistake — and wonders if 'a part of him made the mistake on purpose' to preserve his narrative
jokes.explanation: Michael committing an obvious workplace crime and then philosophizing about whether his mistake was 'on purpose' is both funny and revealing. Toby's point — 'you don't make a mistake on purpose, then it's no longer a mistake' — is a rare moment of Toby being sharp.

jokes.text: Michael's final confession: 'I wanna mess everything up so I can fix it and keep my job.' / Toby: 'Good thing I'm here, 'cause I do nothing. I make everybody nervous.'
jokes.setup: Michael has had an accidental breakthrough, revealing his self-sabotage psychology
jokes.punchline: Michael's genuine self-analysis is immediately undercut by Toby's self-deprecating 'I do nothing. I make everybody nervous' — Toby absorbing his own uselessness
jokes.explanation: Michael's accidental therapy breakthrough is excellent — 'I wanna mess everything up so I can fix it and keep my job' is genuine insight delivered accidentally. Toby's self-aware 'I do nothing, I make everybody nervous' is a great button — he's had a breakthrough too, which is that he's ineffective. Two characters revealing truth simultaneously.

jokes.text: Michael's confessional about Toby: 'Good thing I'm here, 'cause I do nothing. I make everybody nervous. Aah!'
jokes.setup: Michael reflects on Toby's role in the office
jokes.punchline: Michael accurately describes himself while thinking he's describing Toby — the 'Aah!' seems to be a jump-scare he inflicts on himself or a theatrical gesture
jokes.explanation: The self-projection joke appears again but less sharply than #67. The 'Aah!' is a funny physical button but the writing is thinner here.

jokes.text: Michael's doodles during therapy: 'That's the office, huh? Look at that. Angela's cat. Why is Angela taller than Dwight?'
jokes.setup: Michael has been drawing during the session instead of engaging
jokes.punchline: His office drawing is apparently crude and scale-incorrect; he himself doesn't know why he drew Angela taller than Dwight
jokes.explanation: Michael's bewilderment at his own drawing choices is funny. The detail of Angela's cat being included, and Michael's own confusion about the Angela-Dwight scale issue, is a nice small character beat.

jokes.text: Michael: 'Psychiatrists tend to be more crazy than their patients. Therapists are whores. Psychiatry is a narcissism machine.'
jokes.setup: Michael is apparently riffing on anti-therapy slogans while Toby is there
jokes.punchline: The escalating list of anti-psychiatry takes, delivered as brainstorming, culminates in 'psychiatry is a narcissism machine' — an accidentally self-aware statement from one of television's great narcissists
jokes.explanation: 'Psychiatry is a narcissism machine' said by Michael Scott is rich with dramatic irony. He would know. The three-part escalating list is well-structured and the final item lands best.

jokes.text: Michael: 'I learn more from Dr.** than from Dr. Froyd.' / 'Earth. You don't have to be crazy to live here. But it helps.' / 'I don't know... just use the best one.'
jokes.setup: Michael is apparently auditioning anti-therapy bumper sticker slogans
jokes.punchline: The mispronunciation of Freud as 'Froyd,' the pivot to a bumper sticker about Earth, and the final directive 'just use the best one' reveal Michael is workshopping copy for... something
jokes.explanation: 'Dr. Froyd' is a nice malapropism. The 'Earth — you don't have to be crazy to live here, but it helps' bumper sticker is an old joke Michael is treating as fresh material. The sign-off 'just use the best one' reveals he's been brainstorming anti-therapy slogans throughout the session, which is a funny character revelation.

tmdb_overview: Corporate assigns Michael to counseling with Toby. Dwight vows revenge on the Steamtown Mall after a shop owner snubs him. Meanwhile, Pam conspires to change her job title.
